The equivalence applies to the utilization-sensitive compute fleet rather than to all capex, so the dollar figure is an order-of-magnitude translation rather than a precise forecast, but the percentage is exact under the identity. The figure is gross rather than net: raising utilization carries its own cost, in scheduling and orchestration software, networking, and engineering effort, so the capital actually freed is somewhat smaller, though those costs typically run well below the capacity they displace.

Figure 1. Capital released by raising effective utilization above a 20% baseline, holding capability fixed, from equation (4). Marked points show the saving at target utilizations of 30, 40, 50, and 55 percent. The annotation translates the percentage into dollars against an illustrative compute-hardware base of $290 billion.

How much rests on the 20% figure. Because baseline utilization is the most contested input in the paper, it is worth showing that the conclusion does not hinge on it. The percentage in equation (4) is exact and depends only on the two utilization levels, not on any dollar assumption. Table 3 evaluates it across the plausible range.

Even at a pessimistic 25% baseline, lifting utilization to 40% frees more than a third of the compute-capital base, and at the contested 20% it frees half. Translating to dollars introduces the one soft assumption, the compute-hardware share of capex: applying a 35% target to a base of $246 billion to $336 billion, which is 55% to 75% of the 2025 five-firm total, frees roughly $70 billion at the conservative end and $190 billion at the aggressive end, with the $124 billion headline near the middle. The qualitative claim, that a utilization gain is worth tens to nearly two hundred billion dollars of avoided capacity, survives the full range of inputs.

Capability under a scaling law. The results so far hold for any monotonic f. Giving f an explicit form lets the model speak to capability directly. The scaling-laws literature finds that the reducible part of training loss falls as a power of the compute used to train a model [49,50]. Writing reducible loss as L and, in this training-compute regime, effective compute as E, L(E) = γ · E⁻ᵅ (6) with an empirical exponent α that is small, roughly 0.05 in the original estimates [49] and nearer 0.15 once compute is allocated optimally between model size and data [50]. Two consequences follow. First, the utilization gain of equation (4) carries a capability reading as well as a capital one. Holding capex fixed, raising effective utilization from u₀ to u₁ multiplies E by u₁/u₀ and lowers reducible loss by the factor (u₁/u₀) raised to the power minus α; a move from 20% to 35%, a factor of 1.75, cuts reducible loss by 3% to 8% at no additional capital. Second, the parity condition becomes a statement about gaps. If actor A commands R times the effective compute of actor B, the reducible loss of A is only R raised to the power minus α times that of B, Lₐ/Lᵦ = R⁻ᵅ (7)

When capability responds to compute with a small exponent, the marginal return to raw scale is low, and the return to
, which multiplies effective compute directly, is correspondingly high.

It is also why a constrained competitor can stay within striking distance of a far larger one, the pattern the DeepSeek episode displayed. A caveat of regime applies: these exponents describe pre-training, whereas the newer paradigm of inference-time, or test-time, compute follows its own scaling curve. The capital-efficiency identity is indifferent to which regime dominates, since inference compute already enters through utilization, but equation (6) should be read as the pre-training law and not the test-time one.
